records.caption:
One of my favorite soul records of all time ! I bought this while record hunting in Wisconsin and really came to fall in love with it. Very catchy & fun tune u can listen to anytime of the day. I’m usually not a huge fan of the more refined, soft and sweet 70s soul sound, but this one rlly caught my ears.

This single is by the “Supurbs” (only known recording from them) on the Al-teen record, which was active during the 6-70s in the Chicago ~ Milwaukee soul scene. Couldn’t track down any of the members in the “Supurbs” so I’d appreciate if anyone knows anything of them!
records.label: Alteen
records.research: Cataloged by a soul record dealer and collector discussion; artist spelling and exact pressing color vary.

records.caption:
Skip ahead to slide 4 if you want to hear the music!

I’ll admit this record was a bit of an accident (…) I picked it up in a dollar bin thinking it was Blind Blake, the Piedmont blues guitarist from Jacksonville, Florida. Instead, it turned out to be Blind Blake Alphonso Higgs, the Bahamian calypso musician. At first I was embarrassed by the mix-up, but honestly, it’s hard to feel disappointed once you listen. Both “Blakes” are remarkable in their own right, and it’s almost as if the name itself carries a certain musical magic. (At first I figured he must’ve taken his name from the bluesman, but nope, they just happen to share the same name, and both were blind.)

What struck me most was Higgs’ banjo playing - lightning-fast, playful, and irresistibly rhythmic. Even within the distinctly Caribbean flavor of his calypso recordings, you can hear the echoes of American folk and blues traditions. Given the Bahamas’ geographic and cultural closeness to the U.S., that overlap feels natural… Anyways this record is extremely great and can’t recommend it enough!! 😍😍 My favorite track on this is “J P Morgan” and “Jones Oh Jones”
records.title: J P Morgan / Jones Oh Jones (featured songs)
records.research: The post specifically names “J P Morgan” and “Jones Oh Jones” as favorite tracks. Both are documented songs performed by Blind Blake (Alphonso Higgs). Without confirming the photographed edition, these are not assigned as the two sides of this copy.

records.caption: Released in 1961 in Lakeland, Florida, this is the only record ever put out on the Nicktone label! Side A, “Always Alone,” is straight honky-tonk country and sounds uncannily like Lefty Frizzell (could be just coincidence, or Nicks took after the name from him?). Side B, “Model A Ford Blues,” is the real reason I wanted this record: it’s that perfect mix of “hillbilly” stomp with just enough rock edge to land right in my sweet spot. Also the slightly funky guitar on this side rlly gives it a unique character.
records.artist: Lefty Nicks and His Southern Drifters
records.label: Nicktone
records.research: The label photograph reads NICKTONE RECORD CO., Lakeland, Florida, CP-6019, SIDE 1, “ALWAYS ALONE,” LEFTY NICKS AND HIS SOUTHERN DRIFTERS. The collector caption provides the flip “Model A Ford Blues” and gives 1961. The CP-6019 printed number may be a matrix rather than a label catalog number.
records.matchStatus: artist, label and A-side from photo; B-side from caption

records.caption:
I don’t usually go out of my way to pick up soul-funk records, as my collection lean way more country and rockabilly, but every now and then something cuts through.

I first heard this one at Groove Merchant in SF. That chorus “MISERY LOVES COMPANY” completely hooked me. Tried to buy it on the spot, but it was part of a personal NFS stack, so it just sat in my head for months. I finally found a copy at an old record shop in south-ish end of Chicago ^_^

What’s fascinating is that The Illusions seem to be a garage rock band (?), yet the track leans hard into soul. I love how the super funky vocals are performed onto a rougher, rock-driven instrumental. It gives the whole thing this slightly off-kilter energy that really works. The B-side, “Give Me Mercy,” really shines on the guitars that are super rhythmic, almost hypnotic in a sense. 

The label itself comes out of St. Louis, run by Matt McKinney (named after his wife, Jessica). He was connected with Harvey Fuqua and apparently had ambitions of breaking into the Motown… which obviously did not happen lol

Anyways both sides an absolute stomper and a great record highly recommend
records.label: Essica
records.research: Cataloged as Essica 002 (1966); A/B order follows the discography, which differs from the wording in the user's caption.

records.caption:
I’ve always loved country songs that deal with the “devil” because they reveal that deeper, darker side of country music that never shies away from life’s rougher edges. “Devil Train” is one of those killer creepy tracks. It was recorded by Darryl Humphrey under the pseudonym Johnny Doe, and he has a great deep voice that goes well with the theme.

It’s worth noting that this isn’t the same “Johnny Doe” as Stan Furlow, who also used that name and happened to cover the same track in the ’70s!!
records.title: Devil Train (side A shown)
records.research: The yellow label photo shows “DEVIL TRAIN” (Darryl Humphrey) by JOHNNY DOE, with catalog marking AS 517-A and an AIS/AS Records imprint. The original caption clarifies this Johnny Doe is Darryl Humphrey, not Stan Furlow. The flip title remains unidentified.
records.label: AIS Records (as printed)
records.matchStatus: visible title, pseudonym, writer and A-side from photo

records.caption:
Though I haven’t stopped buying records (I still have a whole box of rare 45s I haven’t even logged yet 😅) I’ve been going through some big life changes lately, including moving to a new place and starting a new job, so I haven’t been quite as active here.

Anyhow… this is “Bright Light, Big Star” / “Heart of Gold” by Virgil Weaver on Blue Valley Records. I’m familiar with the Blue Valley label associated with MGM, but this particular imprint seems to be much more obscure. There’s very little information about it online, though it was likely a small local Michigan label, since the record was cut at MCM Studios in Mt. Clemens, Michigan. As far as I can tell, this was the only record ever released by Virgil Weaver, and I haven’t been able to find any other recording credits for its producer, Ron Darlin, either. He had such a great voice though, hopefully there’s some other cut of him out there … If anyone has any info on Blue Valley Records please let me know! Would appreciate it 🙏

records.research: The photograph shows the A-side “BRIGHT LIGHT BIG STAR” credited to Virgil Weaver on Blue Valley. The original collector caption supplies the flip “Heart of Gold” and describes MCM Studios in Mt. Clemens, Michigan. The exact catalog number and pressing date remain unconfirmed.

records.caption: One of my absolute favorite niches to collect on vinyl is Halloween-inspired, horror-themed music (!!) the stranger, the better. Out of all the spooky novelty records I’ve come across, this one is the one that kicked off my fixation. I loooove the raw character this record have … the eerie atmosphere, tongue-in-cheek charm, and an unbelievably catchy hook that lodges itself in your brain - “i belong to the BEEEEAT GENERATION.” I also love the saxophone at the end-ish of this track.. scratches the right part of my brain ^_^
records.research: The quoted “I belong to the Beat Generation” lyric and Halloween theme identify the song with Bob McFadden & Dor (Rod McKuen). The US Brunswick 9-55140 couples “The Mummy” with “The Beat Generation” (1959). Exact pressing of the photographed copy has not been independently compared to its label.
records.label: Brunswick

records.caption:
Haven’t posted in a while, but I definitely haven’t stopped collecting records lol

On a trip to Detroit a little while back, I went digging for records, and this one ended up being my favorite find from the whole trip!! The label alone,, Ranger Records already got me (the artist’s name is Forrest Green… on Ranger…). But the record itself is also very charming. Side A is this quirky, upbeat country tune, and Side B flips into a slow, mellow ballad. Forrest Green has such a great smooth voice that I’ll never get tired of. There’s also a female duet on both tracks that I lovee which I’m guessing it’s his wife. It’s very sweet !!

Forrest Green is also a quite accomplished and prominent figure in the country scene, having recorded in the infamous Owen Bradley’s “hut studio” and performing in the grand ole opry shows along side big names. Forrest founded the “Ranger” label himself in 1954, along with his first recording studio. He spent decades producing, arranging, and recording hundreds of songs, not just his own, but also for countless regional artists, plus handful of major names like Warner Mack and Helen Carter. At one point he even had his own TV series and a long-running touring show, The Forrest Green Show.

Anyways hope you all give it a spin it’s quite a great country track ^_^

records.caption:
I’m a big fan of rockabilly that flirts more with the “hillbilly” side than the “rock” side … and despite its title, the A-side track “Gotta Rock” definitely hits that sweet spot. This particular copy is a 1970s reissue from Olympic Records, originally released in 1956 by Stardale Records, a label started by Dale Davis himself out in Oklahoma. Prob has some personal significance to him as this was the very first single he put out on his own label. 
Bought at @rooky_ricardos_records thanks!

records.caption: I always like picking up a record from the Ark Records label when I come across one. This is the only record Bob Landy ever made, which is a shame because I really love his lush, deep voice. It has the same smooth, emotional quality that reminds me of Lefty Frizzell. A great country ballad.

records.caption:
A lot of folks know J.J. Cale as the great legend behind the Tulsa Sound, with a hit career that stretched from the late 1950s all the way to his posthumous releases in 2019. But not many realize his very first appearance on record came way back in 1958, when he was still going by Johnny Cale. That year, he played lead guitar on a rare 45 rpm single featuring two tracks by Al Sweatt: “I Hate Myself” and “Paint the Town Red.”

This single comes with a quite a hefty price tag, not just because of its rarity, but because it marks the start of Cale’s recording career. On “I Hate Myself,” the guitar riff towards the end is especially memorable. It’s got a sharp swing to it: punchy, clean, and already showing signs of the cool, understated style Cale would later be known for. The B-side, “Paint the Town Red,” is a rougher, more driving rockabilly number that’s full of raw energy.

While Cale went on to shape an entire sound and influence artists like Clapton and Knopfler, Al Sweatt didn’t stick around the music scene for long. After this single, he took more than a decade off to focus on his family and only made a short-lived return in the ‘70s. It’s a bit of a shame as both tracks are fantastic, and his songwriting had real spark... 😞
records.artist: Al Sweatt (with Johnny Cale and the Valentines)

records.caption:
Larry Lee Phillipson is perhaps best known for his early rockabilly hit “Bitter Feelings,” recently reissued by the infamous Numero Group. But a decade after that breakout single, Phillipson released his versions of “The Interstate Is Coming Through My Outhouse” and “The Prisoner’s Song” - a noticeable shift in tone and style. These later tracks showcase a more mature voice and a deeper commitment to traditional country music, revealing an artist who had grown significantly since his rockabilly days.

Also to note, Larry Lee Phillipson is a life-long Milwaukee resident. What’s always struck me is how unexpectedly rich Milwaukee’s country music scene is. While cities like Nashville or Austin are typically top of mind when talking about country, Milwaukee has quietly cultivated its own tradition. I’ll be posting more Milwaukee based country 45s…
records.a: The Interstate Is Coming Through My Outhouse

records.caption:
I’m sure a lot of you can relate to this fine tune given the current economic situation 😪 Buck Griffin certainly could. Music always had to take a back seat to earning a living. He spent time digging pipeline ditches in Kansas and eventually worked his way up to become a driller in the oil fields.

Luckily, the oil fields were surrounded by fantastic honky tonk bars that gave him a way back into music. During the day, he worked in the fields, and at night, he performed at the local bars. He struggled financially throughout his career and never quite made it big, but certainly he was a talented songwriter and performer.

What I love most is the charm that comes through in all of his songs, carrying this distinctive southern twang.
records.research: The photograph shows the blue Lin Records label, 45-1007-B, “One Day After Pay-Day” by Buck Griffin. The Lin discography confirms “Rollin' Tears” as the A-side and an October 1954 release. The original caption's discussion of income and working in the oil fields corresponds to the song.
records.label: Lin

records.caption: If you know me, you know I can’t resist a strange outsider record - and this one’s another gem. Released by a small label called Narrow Way Gospel Line out of Spanish Town, Jamaica, it’s oddly comforting and deeply nostalgic. The lo-fi production and off-key group vocals evoke the scene of a Sunday school class led by a passionate teacher.

records.caption:
Great Appalachian-leaning folk record from the Hill-Dillies. I picked it up originally for Side A, The Eden Valley Fox Hunt, which delivers exactly what you’d hope: lively & playful with a raw, regional charm. But after listening to it at home, Side B really grew on me. I’m a hugeee sucker for train sounds on records and this one nails it. 

Assuming it’s a custom press, with the artist name doubling as the label, and one of only two known releases from Minnesota’s WJON Broadcasting Co.
records.research: A collector's detailed discussion names the B-side as “The Wabash Cannon Ball” and dates the custom disc to 1969, with WJON Broadcasting copyright credit. This matches the train sounds mentioned in the original caption. The exact catalog number has not been confirmed.
records.label: The Hill-Dillies (custom pressing)

records.caption:
One of my favorite finds today while rummaging through the dollar bins on the South Side of Chicago. Side A is a solid rockabilly cut, but the B-side, “Voices of Arizona,” is a clearrr stand out 

It’s a bittersweet country song about trying to “make it big” in Chicago, but coming up short…broke, homesick, and feeling like a disappointment. Pretty ironic as the artist sings about failing to make it, and this record, likely his only one, wounded up forgotten in a bargain bin.

The label, Jorel, only released a few records across an odd mix of genres around Chicagoland. Wonder why this guy decided to do country in Chicago out of all the places.

#45 #countrymusic #countrymusicfan #vinyljunkie #45rpmclub #45rpm #vinyl #vinylrecord

records.caption:
Such a cool little record from Jimmie Dawson!! Hot Tamale Wagon b/w If I Can’t Have You came out around 1957 in Savanna, Illinois on the Pla Boy label and it’s just a great slice of small-town rockabilly. Hot Tamale Wagon is the wild one here, an extremely catchy bopper with this strange, super-repetitive hook that somehow totally works, while the flip If I Can’t Have You slows things down for a straight, heartfelt country ballad. I wonder if Savanna has a significant Hispanic population, which would make sense as to him to writing about tamales 😆 

This 45 also shows up on two other tiny local labels, (Iowans and Jimmy Dawson Sings) with the same master, probably just reorders or rebrands for different local markets, which was pretty common with private press records back then.
records.label: Pla-Boy
records.research: Multiple contemporary small-label issues existed; Pla-Boy 45-806 is separately cataloged, but exact release year is uncertain.
